summary: Presents conservative methods of using TCP DSACKs and SCTP duplicate TSN notifications to identify unnecessary retransmissions for various applications. Both protocols tell the sender when a segment arrived more than once. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a sender repeats a message that already arrived. The receiver says it got two copies, and this explains how the sender can use that hint to learn it repeated too soon.

questions: how to use dsack for congestion control
subtitle: Identifying wasted retransmissions using duplicate notifications

tldr.problem: A TCP or SCTP sender sometimes sends a segment again even though it already arrived, causing wasted bandwidth. The receiver can detect these unnecessary retransmissions by announcing duplicate arrivals.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC presents conservative algorithms to interpret duplicate notifications (DSACKs in TCP, duplicate TSNs in SCTP) to distinguish real packet loss from false alarms caused by network reordering or other factors.
tldr.outcome: A sender can now use these algorithms to avoid incorrectly reverting congestion control changes when a retransmission was actually unnecessary, improving network efficiency.

today: RFC 3708 is an Experimental specification that has not been obsoleted. It defines conservative algorithms for safely using duplicate notifications to detect spurious retransmissions without incorrectly reducing congestion control.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TCP and SCTP both support mechanisms for the receiver to report when it receives a duplicate segment: Duplicate Selective Acknowledgement (DSACK) in TCP and Duplicate Transmission Sequence Number (TSN) notification in SCTP. When a segment arrives more than once, the receiver sends this notification back to the sender.

The sender can use these notifications to detect spurious retransmissions—segments that were sent again unnecessarily because the sender believed they were lost when they actually arrived the first time. This RFC outlines two conservative approaches: one for simple counting of spurious events for monitoring, and a second algorithm designed to safely undo congestion control changes that were made in response to a retransmission that did not indicate real loss.
sections.eli5: The receiver says "I got that message twice." The sender can use this hint to figure out if it retransmitted too soon.

sections.title: Counting Spurious Retransmissions
sections.content:
The simplest application of duplicate notifications is to count how many segments were retransmitted unnecessarily. A sender can track every time a duplicate notification arrives for a previously retransmitted segment, giving it a count of spurious retransmissions.

This count is useful for monitoring and adapting transport algorithms. For example, some TCP improvements (such as Early Retransmit, which triggers faster retransmission with fewer duplicate ACKs) could be tuned by observing the spurious retransmission rate. If the rate is high, the algorithm may be too aggressive. This counting method works reliably across both TCP and SCTP without additional complexity.
sections.eli5: Keep score of how many times you sent something twice by mistake. If the number gets too high, you know your guessing is too trigger-happy.

sections.title: Congestion-Loss Disambiguation Algorithm
sections.content:
The RFC's second and more sophisticated algorithm lets the sender safely revert congestion control changes when it detects a spurious retransmission. The key challenge is distinguishing between two scenarios: (a) a real loss occurred in the network (congestion), and (b) the sender simply transmitted too fast. A sender must not undo congestion control reductions if real loss occurred, even if some individual segments were spuriously retransmitted.

The algorithm works by tracking which segments have been retransmitted and checking incoming duplicate notifications. The sender maintains a scoreboard (as defined in RFC 3517 for TCP) that records the status of segments. When a duplicate notification arrives, the algorithm checks whether the segment was retransmitted exactly once. If it was retransmitted multiple times or not retransmitted at all, the algorithm stops and does not revert congestion control. This conservative approach ensures safety.

Additionally, the algorithm checks whether all retransmitted segments in a window of data have been acknowledged as duplicates. Only if every retransmitted segment received a duplicate notification can the sender conclude that the entire window contained only spurious retransmissions and no real loss.
sections.eli5: Before giving up your caution, check every retransmit in a batch: did they all come back as duplicates? If even one segment was truly lost, keep being cautious.

sections.title: Security and Network Duplication
sections.content:
The main security concern is that a malicious or buggy receiver could falsely report duplicate notifications, tricking a sender into believing it did not lose a segment when it actually did. This could cause the sender to send at an inappropriately high rate, potentially overwhelming the network.

The RFC notes that packet duplication in the network is rare (less than 1% of packets), so the algorithm does not attempt to distinguish between spurious retransmissions and network duplication of original segments. Instead, if the algorithm detects network duplication (a duplicate notification for a segment that was never retransmitted), it disables itself for the remainder of the connection. Future extensions, such as using TCP timestamps to add more evidence, could allow continued use of the algorithm even with network duplication present.
sections.eli5: A dishonest receiver could fake duplicate reports and make you send too fast. The algorithm is designed to stop itself if it detects something fishy.

sections.title: Related Detection Methods
sections.content:
Several alternative approaches exist for detecting spurious retransmissions. The Eifel detection algorithm (RFC 3522) uses TCP timestamps to determine whether an ACK is for an original transmission or a retransmission, enabling faster and more precise detection. However, Eifel requires the 12-byte timestamp option on every packet. The F-RTO scheme observes the pattern of ACKs after a retransmission timeout to infer whether the timeout was spurious, but it only detects spurious timeout-based retransmissions, not those triggered by duplicate ACKs. Time-based heuristics that compare the time between a timeout retransmit and the next ACK to a fraction of the minimum RTT have also been explored, with mixed accuracy.

The DSACK-based algorithm in this RFC requires no additional packet overhead beyond duplicate notifications already defined in TCP and SCTP, making it practical to deploy. It trades off some detection speed and precision for simplicity and safety.
sections.eli5: Other ways to detect mistakes exist, but this one is simple and does not need extra stuff in every packet.
